lastText: File ClosedWhat the Steppe KeptContestedSoviet High Command, 1939–1945End of hostilities: NOVEMBER 1945 (PROJECTED) · filed late, out of sequenceImmediate AftermathVictory in Europe arrives around November 1945: later than the historical May 1945, the price of choices that spent time to save men. The army that reaches Berlin has paid for the ground twice over: a war fought closer to the historical pattern of holding rigid lines regardless of the arithmetic, at the cost this campaign keeps returning to. The tank armies waited for the three fronts to close together and entered Prague on May 11, two days later than they did in the real war. The Seelow Heights fell on the second day instead of the third, at a lower cost: the best the plan could have done, and not what happened. Operation Mars was scaled back rather than launched at full strength: sparing the Rzhev grinder's historical cost, a battle Soviet archives themselves stayed quiet about for fifty years. No branch of this campaign reaches a different destination, only the timing and the price were ever in Soviet hands.One Year LaterVictory arrived behind the historical May 1945, which means Soviet forces are still consolidating a front the historical record had a year's head start settling by this point.
